title: Kamma in the moment
hook: the "impulsion" moments where intention does its work

segments.voice: Yesterday, how fast: one moment of matter lasting while seventeen moments of mind arise and pass. Your line: faster than a blink.

A man is asleep under a mango tree with his head covered. A ripe mango drops and brushes past his ear. He wakes, uncovers his head, and looks. He reaches out and picks the fruit up. He squeezes it, sniffs it, decides it's good. Then he eats it. The commentaries tell that simile, and every step in it stands for one stage of a single act of perception. The falling fruit, the turning, the looking, the testing. But only one step is the eating. Today, the eating.
screen: `ASLEEP UNDER A MANGO TREE.` → `LOOK, PICK IT UP, TEST IT.` → `THEN HE EATS.`

segments.voice: When something strikes a sense door, the Abhidhamma says, the mind runs a set series of moments. It turns toward the object. It sees, or hears. It receives, investigates and settles what the thing is. None of that is kamma yet. It's the man waking, looking, testing. Then come the moments the manual calls javana, usually translated impulsion, or running. In an ordinary sense process they usually run seven times in a row. This is the eating: where the mind doesn't only know the mango but takes it, likes it, wants it, pushes it away, or meets it with kindness. And this is where the manual locates kamma. Back on day three hundred seventy-two, you met the Buddha's plain words: intention is what I call kamma; having intended, a person acts by body, speech and mind. The Abhidhamma gives that sentence an address. Kamma isn't stored in some far-off ledger. It's made in these few running moments, wholesome or unwholesome, again and again, all day. So javana is where a life changes direction. You can't stop the mango from falling. You can't unsee it. But a pause, a breath, a moment of knowing what you're about to do, and the next run of javana can go a different way. After matter, a living body and the speed of it all, this is where the speed turns into a choice.
screen: `TURN, SEE, RECEIVE, SETTLE.` · `THEN JAVANA RUNS.` · `INTENTION IS KAMMA.` · then, large: `THE PAUSE BEFORE THE TAKING.`

segments.voice: Sit still and wait for an impulse: to scratch an itch, shift your weight, open your eyes, check the time. When it comes, don't follow it right away; name it quietly, wanting to move, and feel what happens in the pause. Then, if you choose to, move, knowing that you're moving.
Javana. Impulsion, the running moments after the mind knows its object, where intention does its work and kamma is made. Today's word.
Your line: where kamma is made. The mango falls either way; the taking is where a life turns. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Theravada Abhidhamma study, students learn the series of mind-moments in a sense process, often through the commentaries' mango simile, and teachers point to the javana moments as the place where kamma is made.

fork.setup: you're the man under the mango tree. the fruit has fallen, you've looked at it and tested it. in the simile, which step stands for javana?
fork.reveal: the eating. the waking, looking and testing stand for the stages before; the eating is javana, the moments that take the object.

chat.says: If kamma is about what we do, where exactly does it get made?
options: In javana, the running moments after the mind knows a thing, where intention takes it up.
In the first flash of seeing, before the mind has even settled what it sees.
Only in big deeds done with the body; passing thoughts and words don't count.
chat.meaning: Seeing and settling aren't kamma yet. Kamma is made in javana, where intention works, as the Buddha said: intention is what I call kamma.

javana.meaning: the running moments where intention works and kamma is made

kamma.meaning: action; the Buddha calls intention itself kamma

sense door.meaning: a sense, like the eye or ear, where an object meets the mind

Abhidhamma.meaning: the higher teaching, the third basket of the Pali canon

notes: Week close (days 1079–1085): the teach ends with a one-line look back at the week; confirm it reads naturally.
'Javana usually runs seven times in an ordinary sense process' stated from Abhidhammattha Sangaha IV; confirm.

The mango simile: details vary between tellings (some include the man smelling it, swallowing, then sleeping again). The script tells a simplified version and doesn't map every stage; confirm the source attribution (Atthasalini and the Sangaha commentaries).
'Javana usually translated impulsion, or running': standard renderings; no etymology claimed.
AN 6.63 paraphrased: 'Intention, I tell you, is kamma. Intending, one does kamma by way of body, speech and intellect.' Confirm.
Commentaries hold that the first and seventh javana have special results (in this life / the next); not raised.
